learn.hook: If an atom were the size of a cricket stadium, its nucleus would be a small marble at the centre spot, yet the marble would hold almost all of the stadium's mass.
points: The nucleus is about 10⁴ times smaller than the atom (radius ~10⁻¹⁴ m versus ~10⁻¹⁰ m), but contains more than 99.9% of the atom's mass.
Questions for this chapter: what is a nucleus made of, how big and heavy is it, what holds it together, and how can nuclear energy be released?
Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom = 1.660539 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
Atomic masses are measured precisely with a mass spectrometer.
Non-integral atomic masses arise from isotopes. Chlorine is about 75.4% ³⁵Cl and 24.6% ³⁷Cl, so its average atomic mass is about 35.47 u.

learn.hook: For years, physicists puzzled over why nuclei were heavier than their protons alone. In 1932, James Chadwick found the missing piece: the neutron.
points: The proton is the nucleus of a hydrogen atom, with charge +e and mass about 1.00728 u.

The neutron was discovered by James Chadwick (1932) when beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles and gave out neutral, penetrating radiation. Its mass is about 1.00866 u, slightly more than the proton's.
A nucleus has Z protons (atomic number) and N neutrons; the mass number A = Z + N is the total number of nucleons. It is written ᴬ_Z X (for example ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au).
Isotopes: same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H). Isobars: same A, different Z (³H and ³He). Isotones: same N, different Z (¹⁹⁸₈₀Hg and ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au, both N = 118).
A free neutron is unstable (it decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino), but it is stable inside many nuclei.

topics.title: Size of the nucleus and nuclear density

learn.hook: A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh about a billion tonnes. That is the density of a nucleus, and of a neutron star.
points: From scattering experiments: nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m).
So nuclear volume (4/3)πR³ ∝ A: each nucleon occupies about the same volume.
Nuclear density = mass/volume ≈ (A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷)/((4/3)πR₀³A) is independent of A, about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
This is roughly 10¹⁴ times the density of ordinary matter (water is 10³ kg m⁻³).
Neutron stars are giant 'nuclei' with roughly this density.

learn.hook: Weigh a helium nucleus precisely and you find it lighter than the two protons and two neutrons that make it. The 'missing' mass became binding energy.
points: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence: E = mc². Mass and energy can be converted into each other.
1 u of mass is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy. One gram of matter is equivalent to 10⁻³ × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹³ J.
Mass defect: ΔM = [Zmp + (A - Z)mn] - M, the difference between the total mass of free nucleons and the mass M of the nucleus.
Binding energy Eb = ΔMc²: the energy needed to break the nucleus completely into separate protons and neutrons (or the energy released when they come together).
With atomic masses: ΔM = Z m(¹H) + N mn - m(atom), since electron masses cancel.

topics.title: Binding energy per nucleon and nuclear stability

learn.hook: Plot how tightly each nucleon is held across the periodic table and you get a hill with iron at the summit. Both nuclear power and the Sun's power slide towards that summit.
points: Binding energy per nucleon Ebn = Eb/A measures how tightly a nucleus is bound; larger Ebn means a more stable nucleus.
Ebn versus A curve: it rises steeply for light nuclei, is nearly constant around 8 MeV for 30 < A < 170, peaks near A = 56 (about 8.75 MeV, iron), and falls to about 7.6 MeV for A = 238 (uranium).
The nearly constant Ebn shows the nuclear force is short-range and saturates: each nucleon binds only to its close neighbours.
Heavy nuclei (A > 170) can release energy by splitting into medium nuclei (fission); light nuclei (A < 30) by combining (fusion). In both, Ebn increases.
Example: ¹⁶O with ΔM = 0.13708 u has Eb ≈ 127.7 MeV and Ebn ≈ 7.98 MeV.

learn.hook: Protons in a nucleus are pushed apart by enormous electrical repulsion. Something far stronger glues them together, but only over incredibly tiny distances.
points: The nuclear force binds nucleons together; within its range it is much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion between protons (and vastly stronger than gravity).

It is short-range: strongly attractive at separations of a few femtometres, falling rapidly to zero beyond that. It becomes strongly repulsive when nucleons come closer than about 0.8 fm, which stops the nucleus from collapsing.
It is nearly charge independent: the n-n, n-p and p-p nuclear forces are almost equal.
The potential energy versus separation graph has a minimum near 0.8 fm; to the right the force is attractive, to the left repulsive.
It has no simple formula like Coulomb's law.

example.answer: The nuclear attraction wins over the Coulomb repulsion

learn.hook: Burning a kilogram of coal gives about 3 × 10⁷ J. Fissioning a kilogram of uranium-235 gives about 8 × 10¹³ J, millions of times more.
points: Energy is released whenever nuclei rearrange into products with higher binding energy per nucleon.
Chemical reactions release a few eV per reaction (electrons rearranging); nuclear reactions release MeV per reaction, about a million times more.
Fission: a slow neutron is absorbed by ²³⁵U, forming unstable ²³⁶U, which splits into two medium-mass nuclei plus 2 or 3 neutrons, for example ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴⁴Ba + ⁸⁹Kr + 3n.
Each fission releases about 200 MeV, mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments.
Chain reaction: neutrons from one fission can cause more fissions. Controlled in reactors (power), uncontrolled in a bomb.

teach.nudge: Good! What triggers the split, and why does it release energy?

revise.summary: Nuclear reactions release MeV per event, about a million times more than chemical ones. In fission a slow neutron splits ²³⁵U into two medium nuclei and 2–3 neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV, and the neutrons can sustain a chain reaction.
focus: Why nuclear energy is so large
remember: ~200 MeV per fission, mostly fragment KE
Chain reaction: controlled in reactors, uncontrolled in bombs
traps: Don't guess the number of neutrons; balance the mass numbers
Don't use 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J for 1 MeV; 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J

learn.hook: Every second, the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium. The 'missing' mass becomes the sunlight that warms the Indian monsoon.
points: Fusion: light nuclei combine into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy (for example ²H + ²H → ³He + n + 3.27 MeV).
Nuclei must come very close despite Coulomb repulsion, which needs extremely high temperatures (millions of kelvin). Hence 'thermonuclear' fusion.
In stars like the Sun, the proton-proton cycle converts four protons into one helium-4 nucleus (plus positrons, neutrinos and energy), releasing about 26.7 MeV in total.

Controlled fusion on Earth needs a very hot plasma confined (for example by magnetic fields) long enough; this is very hard. ITER, an international project in France in which India is a partner, is developing a fusion reactor.
Q-value of a reaction: Q = (total initial mass - total final mass) × c² (using 931.5 MeV per u). Q > 0 means energy is released.

example.q: Find the Q-value of ²H + ²H → ³He + n. m(²H) = 2.014102 u, m(³He) = 3.016029 u, mn = 1.008665 u.

learn.reallife: India is a full member of ITER and supplies major in-kind components, such as the giant cryostat (the huge steel vessel around the reactor), whose sections were made in India and then assembled at the ITER site in France.

quiz.q: Why does fusion require very high temperatures?
options: Nuclei need very high kinetic energy to overcome their Coulomb repulsion and come close enough to fuse
quiz.explain: Only at millions of kelvin do nuclei move fast enough.
steps: Nuclei are positively charged and repel
Only at millions of kelvin are they fast enough to come close and fuse
Answer: Nuclei need very high kinetic energy to overcome their Coulomb repulsion and come close enough to fuse
quiz.mistake: Thinks heat is needed to melt

quiz.q: In the proton-proton cycle in the Sun, how many protons are effectively combined to form one ⁴He nucleus?
steps: Net proton-proton cycle: 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + energy

quiz.q: A fusion reaction converts 0.0189 u of mass into energy. What is the Q-value (in MeV, to 2 decimal places)? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
Find the Q-value of ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n: m(²H) = 2.014102 u, m(³H) = 3.016049 u, m(⁴He) = 4.002603 u, mn = 1.008665 u (in MeV, to 2 decimal places).
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the masses the wrong way

quiz.q: A positive Q-value for a nuclear reaction means
options: energy is released (the products have less total mass)
steps: Q > 0 ⇒ products are lighter ⇒ energy released
Answer: energy is released (the products have less total mass)

quiz.q: What is the main challenge in building a controlled fusion reactor?
options: Confining an extremely hot plasma long enough for fusion to occur
quiz.explain: No material wall can hold plasma at millions of kelvin; magnetic confinement is used.
steps: Fusion needs plasma at millions of kelvin
No material wall can hold it; it must be confined (e.g. magnetically) long enough
Answer: Confining an extremely hot plasma long enough for fusion to occur

quiz.q: Which international project, with India as a partner, is building an experimental fusion reactor?
quiz.explain: ITER in France aims to demonstrate fusion power.
steps: The international fusion reactor project in France, with India as a partner

quiz.q: The Sun releases about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus formed. If about 9 × 10³⁷ helium nuclei form each second, what is its power (in units of 10²⁶ W)? (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)
quiz.explain: P = 9 × 10³⁷ × 26.7 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ ≈ 3.84 × 10²⁶ W, close to the Sun's measured output.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert MeV to J

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does the Sun keep shining for billions of years?'
teach.praise: Chirp! In its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium; the lost mass becomes energy by E = mc². Sunshine is nuclear!
teach.nudge: Good! What nuclear process happens in the Sun, and what turns into what?

revise.summary: Fusion joins light nuclei, releasing energy, but needs millions of kelvin to overcome Coulomb repulsion. The Sun's proton-proton cycle turns four protons into helium releasing about 26.7 MeV, and the Q-value is (initial − final mass) × 931.5 MeV.
remember: ITER: international fusion reactor (India a partner)
traps: Fusion needs high temperature, not neutrons, to start
Don't subtract initial from final mass; Q uses initial minus final mass
